docs.title: Glass-to-Glass
docs.text: A camera lens at one end, a display at the other, and a frame that has to cross everything in between. This site follows that path on cheap ARM hardware — what each stage actually costs, where it breaks, and which assumptions stop being true once you measure instead of reading the datasheet.

docs.title: The sections
docs.text:
The pipeline is the project. The other two exist because it needs them.

Video Streaming — the pipeline itself. What a frame is before anyone debayers it, how the kernel exposes the capture hardware, what software encode costs when the board has no encoder, and what a real one buys you.

CI — how it stays honest, because a pipeline nobody tests on real hardware decays without anyone noticing. One pinned toolchain for the laptop and the runner, tests that exercise the kernel boundary with no camera attached, and real boards wired into the pipeline.

Accelerators — the fixed-function silicon every frame crosses or feeds: ISP, video codec, NPU, GPU. Three of the four are closed vendor stacks, and each has already contradicted its own documentation.

docs.title: The boards
docs.text:
Raspberry Pi 5 Orange Pi 6 Plus SoC BCM2712, Cortex-A76 CIX P1 / CD8180 "Sky1" Camera IMX477 and IMX708 over CSI-2 13 MP MIPI-CSI, plus USB Video encode none — there is no encoder on this board Linlon V8, 18 × 1080p30 sustained Inference — Zhouyi V3 NPU, 30 TOPS Camera stack upstream kernel drivers, walkable media graph closed vendor daemon that panics the kernel

That last row is why there are two boards. One has a clean kernel stack and no encoder; the other has a serious hardware encoder and a stack you cannot inspect. Almost everything worth writing down comes out of the gap between them.

docs.title: How to read it
docs.text:
Every number here was measured on a board on my desk, with the date, the kernel and the command recorded. Where something is inferred rather than measured, it says so. Where an earlier version of a page was wrong, the correction stays visible with its date — the refutations tend to be more useful than the claims.

Pages are independent. Each answers one question and states what it does not cover, so there is no reading order and nothing is a prerequisite for anything else.

This is not a tutorial. It assumes Linux, C++, and some exposure to V4L2 or an equivalent driver API, and it spends its time on measured behaviour rather than on abstractions.

Code lives in separate repositories, linked from the pages that discuss it. The implementation language is C++23, built with Bazel. Earlier work was in Rust; where a page still shows Rust, it says so at the top.

docs.title: CI
docs.text:
A video pipeline that nobody tests on real hardware decays without anyone noticing. This section is how the pipeline stays honest.

Embedded CI is usually bad, and the excuses are always the same. Cross-compiling is hard, so we build on the device. On-device tests cannot be automated, because the board is special and the flashing is manual. Neither holds up.

The target: a build on a laptop and a build in CI come out of the same pinned toolchain, through the same scripts, with the same flags — and CI does the full verification, including tests on real boards, with nobody sitting next to the hardware.

docs.title: Integration Testing for Linux Video Pipelines
Integration Testing for Linux Video Pipelines
docs.text:
Rust original

The code here is Rust, against pi-cam-capture, which is no longer the active implementation. The technique is language-neutral: vivid and the layered test structure apply unchanged to the C++ pipeline, and a C++ version of this page will replace it.

Most embedded Linux projects end up with the same testing setup. Unit tests cover parts of the logic, often in a patchy way, because syscalls and OS behavior are out of scope. Hardware-in-the-loop is used to check that the system works on the real device. Even in theory, this combination is weak and fragile, but in many teams it is still treated as "good enough". The blind spot is always the same. The boundary between user space and the kernel is rarely exercised during normal development, even though that is where a large share of real failures occur.

In Linux-based video systems, most application code does not manipulate pixels directly. It involves negotiating formats via ioctls, allocating and mapping buffers, handling blocking semantics, and interpreting metadata produced by drivers. This boundary is where failures cluster, and it is precisely the part of the system that neither unit tests nor HIL handles well.

Unit tests cannot exercise kernel behavior in any meaningful way. In the best case, they replace file descriptors, ioctls, and device state with mocks, which is fine for checking control flow and error handling. What disappears is the behavior that actually matters in video processing. Buffer queues have ordering and lifetime rules. Some ioctls return success while silently adjusting parameters. Others block depending on the driver's state. Timestamps have specific origins and invariants. These details define how a video device behaves, and a mock cannot realistically reproduce them.

And quite often the result is predictable. Code passes unit tests while embedding incorrect assumptions about alignment, stride, buffer lifetime, or sequencing. These assumptions remain invisible until the first interaction with a real device.

At that point, teams fall back to hardware-in-the-loop testing. HIL does exercise the real kernel interface, but it usually happens late and at a high cost. Access to hardware is often limited, setup can be slow, failures may be non-deterministic, and reproducing issues relies heavily on the physical context. When integration problems arise only at this stage, the iteration process can slow down significantly. Continuous Integration (CI) provides little support in this scenario. While it is sometimes possible to wire HIL into a CI pipeline, it tends to be fragile and hard to maintain reliability, which means these paths are not exercised consistently, and regressions reappear.

This creates a systemic blind spot. Unit tests validate logic in an environment that cannot fail in realistic ways. HIL validates behavior in an environment that is expensive and difficult to automate. The kernel boundary, where most integration bugs originate, remains largely untested during normal development. For Linux video systems, this is not an edge case. It is the dominant failure mode.

This gap is structural, not accidental. It comes from how different test layers interact with the system stack and which boundaries they actually cross.

The diagram shows how coverage is distributed across a Linux video, or any other typical embedded system. Unit tests remain confined to application logic and never cross into the kernel. Hardware-in-the-loop testing exercises the full stack, but it sits outside the normal development loop and is expensive to run continuously. Virtual-device integration tests occupy the middle ground. They drive real syscalls and kernel code paths through emulated drivers, allowing the user-space-to-kernel boundary to be exercised early, repeatedly, and in CI, without relying on physical hardware.

docs.title: Why Linux is unusually amenable to this kind of integration testing
docs.text:
Integration testing with virtual devices usually works on Linux because most hardware interaction already goes through the kernel. From the user space, the boundary is not registers or buses. It is file descriptors, ioctls, memory mappings, and kernel metadata. These boundaries are explicit, documented, and often straightforward to virtualize.

For video capture, the contract is V4L2. V4L2 allows us to discover devices via /dev/video* and to obtain capabilities, formats, and controls via standardized ioctls. Buffers are exchanged via MMAP or USERPTR with well-defined lifetime rules. Metadata such as timestamps and sequence numbers follow documented semantics. At the end, from the user space, a physical camera and a virtual camera look identical as long as they speak the same kernel API. In practice, this is visible directly through standard V4L2 tooling. A real camera and a virtual device appear identical at the kernel boundary.

➜ v4l2-ctl --list-devices
vivid (platform:vivid-000):
        /dev/video2

Integrated Camera: Integrated C (usb-0000:00:14.0-6):
        /dev/video0

Such contracts are a key difference from bare-metal or tightly coupled firmware systems. In Linux, the kernel already sits between your code and the hardware, enforcing an abstraction. That abstraction can often be backed by a real driver or a virtual one with identical user-space behavior. As long as the driver implements the same V4L2 contract, the application code exercises the same paths.

Linux also exposes enough system state to enable deterministic discovery and selection. Sysfs provides device identity, driver names, and topology under /sys/class. Procfs exposes the runtime context that affects behavior. Instead of guessing which /dev/video0 is present, code and tests can identify devices by driver and capabilities, and fail explicitly when expectations are not met.

This makes Linux an incredibly practical test harness that helps to keep your codebase stable. Your integration tests are production-like in the sense that you can run real syscalls, negotiate real formats, allocate real buffers, and observe real blocking behavior without needing physical hardware attached. The kernel enforces the same rules either way.

For video systems, this matters in practice. Most integration failures are not sensor-specific. They come from incorrect assumptions about format negotiation, buffer handling, timing, or sequencing. These failures live at the kernel interface. Exercising that interface deterministically catches a large class of bugs early.

docs.title: Making the environment deterministic
docs.text:
Integration tests that touch kernel interfaces only make sense if the environment is predictable. If setup depends on manual steps or undocumented assumptions, failures become ambiguous and easy to dismiss. This is where many teams stop trusting integration tests altogether.

For V4L2, the environment includes user space tools, kernel support, and the way devices appear under /dev and /sys. In this project, those assumptions are encoded directly in a setup script rather than documented separately.

The script starts by installing and verifying the required user space tooling. If inspection tools are missing, there is no point in proceeding.

for cmd in v4l2-ctl ffmpeg; do
    if command -v "$cmd" &>/dev/null; then
        success "$cmd installed"
    else
        error "$cmd not found"
        ok=false
    fi
done

Kernel support is checked explicitly. Virtual devices only work if the driver is available for the running kernel, and this varies by distribution.

for mod in vivid v4l2loopback; do
    if modinfo "$mod" &>/dev/null; then
        success "$mod module available"
    else
        warn "$mod module not available"
    fi
done

Loading the virtual camera is a deliberate step with fixed parameters. The configuration is part of the test contract, not an implementation detail.

$SUDO modprobe vivid n_devs=2 node_types=0x1,0x1 input_types=0x81,0x81

After loading the module, the script validates the result from user space. Tests do not assume devices exist; they require them.

$SUDO v4l2-ctl --list-devices

At this point, the environment is in a known state. Virtual video devices exist, they are discoverable through standard V4L2 tooling, and they expose the same kernel interfaces as physical cameras. Integration tests can rely on this without special casing or fallback logic.

The script also configures deterministic test patterns on each vivid device, using sysfs to identify them and v4l2-ctl to apply known formats and patterns.

if v4l2-ctl -d "$dev" --set-fmt-video=width=640,height=480,pixelformat=YUYV; then
    success "$dev: Set format to 640x480 YUYV"
fi

v4l2-ctl -d "$dev" --set-ctrl=test_pattern="$pattern"

This ensures that integration tests see predictable frame content, not just “some bytes”.

Finally, teardown is explicit. Kernel state is global, and CI runs must clean up after themselves.

Warning

Kernel state is global. It is safe to run multiple integration tests in parallel on a runner that has been preconfigured with vivid already loaded. CI jobs that load or unload kernel modules must not run concurrently on the same runner.

$SUDO modprobe -r vivid

The result is a setup that either succeeds and is validated, or fails immediately. When an integration test fails, the failure comes from the code under test, not from an unclear or partially configured environment.

docs.title: Using kernel-provided virtual devices (vivid)
docs.text:
With a deterministic environment in place, the next question is what the integration tests should talk to. For V4L2, the choice is straightforward. Mock devices in user space do not exercise the kernel boundary. Physical cameras reintroduce cost and instability. The practical middle ground is to use a kernel driver that implements the same V4L2 contract as real hardware.

On Linux, that driver is vivid.

From user space, the application does not talk to hardware directly. It talks to the V4L2 API. Whether the request is handled by a physical camera driver or a virtual one is an implementation detail hidden behind the kernel interface.

This is why vivid works for integration testing. It registers /dev/video* nodes and implements the same ioctls, buffer APIs, and metadata semantics as real capture devices. The code under test follows the same execution paths either way.

This equivalence is visible directly through standard tooling. A physical camera and a vivid device are discovered in the same way:

➜ v4l2-ctl --list-devices
vivid (platform:vivid-000):
        /dev/video2

Integrated Camera: Integrated C (usb-0000:00:14.0-6):
        /dev/video0

Capabilities are queried through the same ioctls and expose the same capture and streaming flags:

➜ v4l2-ctl --device=/dev/video0 --all
Driver name   : uvcvideo
Capabilities  : Video Capture, Streaming

➜ v4l2-ctl --device=/dev/video2 --all
Driver name   : vivid
Capabilities  : Video Capture, Streaming

Format negotiation follows the same path as well:

➜ v4l2-ctl -d /dev/video2 --list-formats
[0]: 'YUYV' (YUYV 4:2:2)

From the application’s point of view, there is no special-case logic here. Devices are opened the same way, formats are negotiated through the same ioctls, and frames are streamed using the same buffer APIs. If the driver speaks V4L2 correctly, user space does not care whether frames originate from a sensor or from a kernel generator.

This makes vivid useful for integration testing, but also defines its limits. It does not model sensor quirks, ISP behavior, or vendor-specific timing details. Those belong in hardware-in-the-loop testing. What vivid does cover is the V4L2 surface itself: format negotiation, buffer handling, sequencing, and timing semantics. That is where many integration failures originate.

docs.title: Structuring integration tests around virtual devices
docs.text:
Once vivid is available, the main job is keeping integration tests honest. They should fail when the runner is not prepared, and they should not depend on accidental details like /dev/video0 ordering.

In the repo, that logic lives in one place: a sysfs-backed discovery function plus a couple of “hard requirement” macros. The discovery code reads /sys/class/video4linux/video*/name, filters for devices that contain vivid, then verifies the device can actually be opened before returning it. That avoids probing real cameras and makes failures deterministic.

// This is a snippet but NOT a real code.
fn vivid_devices() -> Vec<u32> {
    (0..10)
        .filter(|i| {
            let name = std::fs::read_to_string(
                format!("/sys/class/video4linux/video{}/name", i)
            ).unwrap_or_default();

            name.to_lowercase().contains("vivid")
                && V4L2Device::open(*i).is_ok()
        })
        .collect()
}

The tests deliberately do not skip when vivid is missing. They panic with an actionable error, because this is the class of failures CI must catch early. The single-device macro is used for general “can open / can stream” tests.

// This is a snippet but NOT a real code.
macro_rules! require_vivid {
    () => {
        vivid_devices()
            .first()
            .copied()
            .expect("vivid device not found; run dev-setup.sh load-vivid")
    };
}

Some tests depend on two devices, because dev-setup.sh configures them with different patterns. That is where require_vivid_pair!() comes in: it asserts a pair exists and returns (devices[0], devices[1]). If the runner only has one vivid node, or vivid was loaded with the wrong parameters, it fails loudly.

// This is a snippet but NOT a real code.
macro_rules! require_vivid_pair {
    () => {{
        let devs = vivid_devices();
        assert!(
            devs.len() >= 2,
            "expected two vivid devices; check vivid module configuration"
        );
        (devs[0], devs[1])
    }};
}

From there, the test body stays intentionally boring: open device, set a known format, create a small stream, pull frames, validate invariants. The format choice is fixed (640x480 YUYV) so that frame sizing and pixel access are stable across runs.

let mut device = V4L2Device::open(device_index).expect("Failed to open vivid device");

let requested = Format::new(640, 480, FourCC::YUYV);
let actual = device.set_format(&requested).expect("Failed to set format");

let mut stream = device.create_stream(4).expect("Failed to create stream");
let frame = stream.next_frame().expect("Failed to capture frame");

One operational detail matters here: these tests are marked #[serial]. Kernel-backed devices are shared state. Even if the runner is “preconfigured”, concurrent open/stream/close sequences against the same nodes tend to create noise. Serializing keeps failures attributable.

#[test]
#[serial]
fn test_vivid_capture_single_frame() { /* ... */ }

The pattern-specific tests show why having a pair matters. The first device is expected to be configured as a gradient, the second as color bars, and the validations fail with messages that point back to the setup script.

let (gradient_device, _) = require_vivid_pair!();
// ...
let result = validate_gradient(&frame, &format);
assert!(result.is_ok(), "Gradient validation failed on first vivid device...");

This structure keeps the integration suite predictable: the environment requirements are explicit, discovery is deterministic, and the tests exercise the same public API surface as production code.

docs.title: Validating frame content and metadata
docs.text:
Streaming frames is a weak signal. A lot of broken pipelines still stream.

The typical failure is boring and expensive: format negotiation succeeds, buffers flow, sizes look right, and nothing errors out. Then someone notices the image is wrong, or timestamps jump, or sequence numbers reset under load. By that point it is usually on hardware, and it is already hard to localize.

Virtual devices help because the output is predictable. That makes it reasonable to assert properties of frames instead of just checking that data exists.

Start with metadata. Sequence numbers should increase. Timestamps should be present and ordered. If this fails, the pipeline is already violating assumptions downstream components rely on.

let frames: Vec<Frame> = (0..5)
    .map(|_| stream.next_frame().expect("capture failed"))
    .collect();

for w in frames.windows(2) {
    assert!(w[1].sequence > w[0].sequence);
    assert!(w[1].timestamp >= w[0].timestamp);
}

Content checks can stay minimal. vivid can generate fixed patterns. A couple of pixel samples are enough to catch the usual class of mistakes: wrong stride, wrong pixel format assumptions, or broken conversion logic.

let (r1, _, _) = frame.pixel_at(10, 10).unwrap();
let (r2, _, _) = frame.pixel_at(200, 10).unwrap();
assert!(r2 > r1);

This is not image quality testing. It is a sanity check that the pipeline interprets the kernel’s buffers the way it thinks it does. Once metadata and minimal content checks are in place, the integration suite stops answering “did we get a frame” and starts answering “did we handle the frame correctly”.

Virtual-device integration tests do not replace unit tests or hardware-in-the-loop testing. Unit tests still cover logic and edge cases. HIL still covers hardware-specific behavior. The integration layer sits in between, exercising real syscalls, ioctls, buffer queues, and timing semantics without depending on physical devices. This catches kernel-boundary failures early and pushes HIL back to what it is good at, rather than using it as the first line of integration testing.

docs.title: Accelerators
docs.text:
Four pieces of fixed-function silicon sit on one of these boards — an image signal processor, a video codec, a neural accelerator and a GPU — and three of the four are reached only through closed vendor software. Every frame crosses at least one of them.

The pattern repeats: the documentation describes an interface, the driver implements something adjacent to it, and the measurement contradicts both.

docs.title: Pages
docs.text: Two ISP Architectures: Pi 5 and Orange Pi 6 Plus — the same MIPI camera on two boards: ten captures out of ten on the Pi 5, six out of ten on the Orange Pi with every failure a board reset, and ten out of ten from a USB camera on that same board. The difference is not the silicon. It is that one kernel describes its hardware and the other hands you a private ioctl and a closed daemon that already owns the capture node.

docs.title: The silicon
docs.text:
Measured on an Orange Pi 6 Plus, CIX P1 / CD8180 "Sky1", vendor image on kernel 6.6.89-cix.

What it is State ISP closed vendor daemon owning the capture device, one private ioctl on the sensor subdev, entities registered with zero pads and zero links measured; compared against the Pi 5's kernel-described stack VPU Linlon V8 — separate encode and decode engines, four advertised hardware session slots measured: 18 × 1080p30 encode sustained, ~537 fps ceiling at 1080p; decode runs one session only NPU Zhouyi V3 — 1 cluster, 3 cores, 4 TECs, 30 TOPS, KMD v5.11.0. Four 1 GiB address windows per ASID, carved by the driver; no per-process MMU, no demand paging, no preemption measured: MobileNet v2 at 1.7–2.7 ms with the CPU idle; Gemma 4 E2B at 2.51 GB zero-copy, prefill 47.3 tok/s, decode 15.38 tok/s, 52% of speculative drafts accepted GPU Immortalis-G720 MC10, 10 cores. Vulkan 1.3.296, OpenGL ES, 5 render nodes present and working; nothing asked of it yet

Two results change how you design around this hardware. Starting an encode while a decode is streaming wedges the decode permanently, in either start order — so the encoder's generosity and the decoder's rigidity cannot be combined. And the NPU's real win is prefill plus leaving twelve CPU cores free, not raw decode throughput, because decode is bandwidth-bound on the same LPDDR regardless of what runs it.

docs.title: Two ISP Architectures - Pi 5 and Orange Pi 6 Plus
MIPI Cameras on Raspberry Pi 5 and Orange Pi 6 Plus: Two ISP Architectures
docs.text:
I have a Raspberry Pi 5 and an Orange Pi 6 Plus side by side, each with a MIPI camera. Both expose /dev/video* nodes and speak V4L2, so on paper both should be boring to capture from.

The Pi was boring: ten rpicam-hello runs, ten captures. On the Orange Pi, ten gst-launch-1.0 v4l2src device=/dev/video9 runs gave me three captures, a mix of hangs, Failed to allocate required memory and has no supported format, and one reboot mid-run. A day later I interleaved every MIPI capture with one from a Logitech C920 on the same board's USB port. MIPI got six out of ten, and all four failures were the board resetting. The C920 got ten out of ten.

So neither the board nor V4L2 is broken. What differs is the architecture of the camera stack: where the sensor knowledge lives, what the kernel tells userspace, and who owns the capture device.

Why bother with the Orange Pi at all: the hardware gap

On paper the boards aren't in the same league. The CIX P1 has an NPU rated at about 30 TOPS (the 45 TOPS on the box counts the CPU and GPU too) and a hardware H.264/H.265 encoder rated up to 8K at 30 fps1. The Pi 5 has neither: no NPU and, unlike the Pi 4, no hardware H.264 encoder, so encoding means libx264 on the CPU2.

The AI HAT+ 2 (Hailo-10H, 40 TOPS INT4, 8 GB of its own RAM3) fills the NPU gap; the original AI HAT+ never interested me. A kit costs about $350 today, and I paid $366 for the whole Orange Pi. Price isn't the real problem, though. The HAT only accelerates inference. Every streamed frame still goes through libx264 on the CPU, and there's no DMA path from camera to accelerator to encoder for the HAT to sit in, so for my experiments there's not much reason to add one.

The Pi wins a lot back on power: it gets by with a small fan, while the Orange Pi needs a blower that wouldn't look out of place in a gaming laptop. On a battery or in a sealed enclosure, that matters more than TOPS.

docs.title: What a MIPI camera stack has to do
docs.text:
The sensor sits on an I²C bus, and everything about it (mode, exposure, gain) is a register write. Raw Bayer pixels come out over CSI-2 into a receiver on the SoC, and the ISP turns them into something usable like NV12 while producing per-frame statistics. 3A (auto exposure, white balance, focus) reads those statistics and writes new settings back to the sensor and the ISP, every frame.

What I²C is

I²C, written I2C in code, is Inter-Integrated Circuit: a slow two-wire bus (clock plus data) Philips designed in the early 1980s. Devices have 7-bit addresses, so 11-001a on the Pi below means bus 11, address 0x1a. At 100 or 400 kHz it can't carry pixels, which is why a camera has two paths: I²C for control (mode, exposure, gain, chip ID) and CSI-2 for frames. Linux sensor drivers live in drivers/media/i2c/, and i2c_master_send(), which puts bytes on the bus, shows up again later.

Both boards run 3A in userspace. What differs is the interface between userspace and the kernel, and how much of the hardware the kernel describes.

docs.title: Raspberry Pi 5: the kernel describes the hardware
docs.text:
Start with the sensors:

$ for s in /sys/class/video4linux/v4l-subdev*; do echo "$(basename $s) $(cat $s/name)"; done
v4l-subdev0 csi2
v4l-subdev1 pisp-fe
v4l-subdev2 imx477 11-001a
v4l-subdev3 csi2
v4l-subdev4 pisp-fe
v4l-subdev5 imx708
v4l-subdev6 dw9807 10-000c

Each sensor model has its own driver at a real I²C address, and that driver owns the mode tables, format negotiation, exposure and gain behind standard subdev operations and controls.

Every block is also an entity in a Media Controller graph. Of the Pi's 44 entities only one sits outside it, the dw9807 focus motor; everything on the capture path is linked. Each camera port is an rp1-cfe graph (sensor, CSI-2 receiver, the PiSP front end that produces statistics, video nodes), and the PiSP back end, a memory-to-memory ISP, has a graph of its own. A client finds a camera's nodes by following links from the sensor instead of guessing /dev/videoN, and the capture node sets V4L2_CAP_IO_MC, the flag that says the topology is configured through the Media Controller4.

libcamera's PiSP pipeline handler does that walking, configures formats pad by pad, sets sensor controls and runs the capture loop. The 3A algorithms come in an IPA module, ipa_rpi_pisp.so, which in my setup is loaded straight into the application's process.

One process owns the session. At idle fuser finds nothing holding any camera node. During a capture rpicam-hello holds every node it needs, with libcamera and the IPA in its own address space, and when it exits they're all free again.

The stack isn't fully upstream: rp1-cfe and pisp_be are in mainline, but the imx708 and imx477 drivers live in Raspberry Pi's own tree5. Every boundary in it is still a mainline interface, and the IPA ships under open licences. libcamera doesn't even require that: an IPA whose .sign signature doesn't validate runs in a separate, isolated process6, so a vendor's closed 3A fits the design.

That's why the Pi holds up: nothing important is private. The kernel describes the sensor, the links, the formats and the controls, so userspace can be libcamera, my own V4L2 code or anything else that speaks the same API.

docs.title: Orange Pi 6 Plus: a daemon and a register pipe
docs.text:
The same idle check on the Orange Pi gives a different answer. Before any capture, fuser already finds the camera node open:

$ sudo fuser -v /dev/video*
                     USER        PID ACCESS COMMAND
/dev/video9:         root       4374 F.... isp_app

isp_app is the vendor's camera daemon, a closed-source binary. systemd starts it through a unit called isp-daemon.service, and from then on isp_app holds /dev/video9 for as long as it runs. No installed package owns the binary or the unit. In the vendor's repository it belongs to cix-isp-umd (UMD is "user mode driver"), and CIX ships the GPU and NPU the same way: a GPL kernel module plus a closed userspace half.

The kernel half is armcb_isp_v4l2, an out-of-tree module in /lib/modules/<version>/extra/. The GPL source is published7, but the loaded module has no srcversion to tie it to that source, so the driver internals below come from the published tree.

docs.title: Where the sensor knowledge went
docs.text:
The sensors are ACPI devices, and all three camera I²C devices bind to one generic driver, imgsensor0, with identical subdev names:

v4l-subdev0 name=sensor0
v4l-subdev1 name=sensor0
v4l-subdev2 name=sensor0

The published driver tree contains no sensor model names at all, so the kernel side doesn't know which sensor is attached. isp_app does: its strings name four OmniVision sensors (ov08d10, ov13850, ov13855, ov13858), and the proprietary package ships tuning files for them. Two of the four have mainline drivers. The vendor stack uses neither.

docs.title: No graph to walk
docs.text:
The driver creates media devices, but look inside one (trimmed):

$ media-ctl -d /dev/media2 -p | grep -E "^- entity|device node name"
- entity 1: armcb-00-vid-cap (0 pad, 0 link)
            device node name /dev/video9
- entity 4: sensor0 (0 pad, 0 link)
            device node name /dev/v4l-subdev2
- entity 5: isp-sub1 (0 pad, 0 link)
            device node name /dev/v4l-subdev3
- entity 6: motor0 (0 pad, 0 link)
            device node name /dev/v4l-subdev4
...

All 13 entities across the three ISP media devices have zero pads and zero links, because the driver never creates any (media_create_pad_link appears nowhere in the source), and /dev/video9 doesn't set V4L2_CAP_IO_MC. There's no graph to walk. The Pi leaves its focus motor outside the graph too, but there it's the only one. Here it's all thirteen.

The subdevs are just as empty. Every v4l2_subdev_ops in the driver fills only .core, and the sensor's core ops hold one ioctl handler:

sensor/armcb_sensor.c

    switch (cmd) {
    case ARMCB_VIDIOC_APPLY_CMD: {
        struct cmd_buf *pcmd_buf = (struct cmd_buf *)arg;

        switch (pcmd_buf->static_info.bus) {
        case HW_BUS_AHB_POWER:
            res |= armcb_imgsens_hw_apply(pcmd_buf, pimgsens_sd);
            break;
        default:
            res |= armcb_isp_hw_apply(pcmd_buf, client);
            break;
        }
        break;
    }
    default:
        return -ENOIOCTLCMD;
    }

/* ... */

static struct v4l2_subdev_ops armcb_imgsens_subdev_ops = {
    .core = &armcb_imgsens_subdev_core_ops,
};

No .pad, no .video, so mainline's v4l2_subdev_call() returns -ENOIOCTLCMD for set_fmt, enum_mbus_code or s_stream before any driver code runs9. A libcamera pipeline handler would have nothing to call.

docs.title: One private ioctl
docs.text:
That one command is how the sensor gets configured. ARMCB_VIDIOC_APPLY_CMD is BASE_VIDIOC_PRIVATE + 2, and BASE_VIDIOC_PRIVATE is 19210, so it's ioctl number 194. The same header also defines ARMCB_VIDIOC_ISP_DMA_COPY as 194 and gives VIDIOC_ARMCB_ISP_STAT_EN number 194 as well, so the number doesn't even identify the command :-D The payload carries bus-specific settings. The I²C one:

common/armcb_isp.h

struct cmd_i2c_setting {
    unsigned int channel;
    unsigned int slave_addr;
    enum drv_direction direct;
    enum drv_addr_type reg_addr_type;
    enum drv_data_type reg_data_type;
    unsigned int reg_addr;
    unsigned int *ptr_user;
    unsigned int val;
    unsigned int delay_us;
};

Slave address, register address, widths and value all come from userspace. The kernel marshals them into bytes and calls i2c_master_send(); a comment in the ordering code says /// already sort in userspace. The driver is a privileged register pipe plus a buffer manager, and the hardware description, register tables, tuning and 3A all live in isp_app.

The capture node shows the same split. /dev/video9 exposes zero V4L2 controls, while the C920 on the same board exposes 23. AE, AWB and AF modes exist only in isp_app's own command language, documented in its -h output.

docs.title: How a capture actually starts
docs.text:
Client and daemon never talk directly. isp_app has no socket or FIFO, just /dev/video9, /dev/null and its journal, so the driver's event queue is their only channel. The daemon's log when a gst-launch client starts, trimmed:

daemon.c Daemon_Subevent_Process(137): VIDIOC_DQEVENT success ret(0)
Daemon_Event_Process enter --->, event_id:108
daemon.c Daemon_Subevent_Process(137): VIDIOC_DQEVENT success ret(0)
Daemon_Event_Process enter --->, event_id:106
app_layer.c App_Layer_Camera_Start(892): camera 0 starting
device_buf_mgr.c Device_Buf_Allocate(379): allocate 5(5) buffers success
app_layer.c App_Layer_Camera_Start(945): camera 0 started
pipeline.c Pipeline_Initialize(1302): cam 0: ... preview[1920*1080] ...
isp_hw_v4l.c Isp_V4l_Open_Subdev(532): open file /dev/v4l-subdev2
isp_hw_v4l.c Isp_V4l_Open_Subdev(532): open file /dev/v4l-subdev3

The client's open, S_FMT and STREAMON become events. The daemon wakes on VIDIOC_DQEVENT, starts camera 0, allocates buffers, initialises its 1080p pipeline and opens the sensor and ISP subdevs. From there, ARMCB_VIDIOC_APPLY_CMD is the only sensor-register path the driver offers. I didn't trace the daemon's syscalls, so that last hop comes from the driver source rather than observation.

docs.title: Why the Orange Pi stack breaks
The kernel panic
docs.text:
The vendor image keeps logs in RAM (orangepi-ramlog) and ramoops caught nothing, so at first the resets left no trace. With a persistent journal I have five panics. Every one faults in the same place, __video_do_ioctl taking a mutex, and three of them look like this:

armcb_v4l2_core.c armcb_g_param (1399): g_param enter
armcb_v4l2_core.c armcb_v4l2_g_selection (1340): enter: target = 257, type = 1
Unable to handle kernel paging request at virtual address 004e495f43455355
Internal error: Oops: 0000000096000004 [#1] PREEMPT SMP
CPU: 10 PID: 5318 Comm: v4l2src0:src Tainted: G S         O
pc : mutex_lock_interruptible+0x10/0x6c
lr : __video_do_ioctl+0xe0/0x3c8
...
Call trace:
 mutex_lock_interruptible+0x10/0x6c
 video_usercopy+0x200/0x760
 video_ioctl2+0x18/0x30
 v4l2_ioctl+0x40/0x60
Kernel panic - not syncing: Oops: Fatal exception

The other two faulted deeper inside the same lock acquisition, one in osq_lock and one in queued_spin_lock_slowpath, under the same __video_do_ioctl call. A mutex whose internal fields are unreadable too isn't a mutex with a bad address. It's memory that stopped being a mutex.

The crash is in the mainline V4L2 core, in GStreamer's capture thread v4l2src0:src, and the core takes that lock before it ever calls the driver11. The mutex address is in x1, the register the fast-path compare-and-swap writes through, and in this trace it's 0x494e495f43455355: text, USEC_INI in little-endian ASCII. (The reported fault address loses the top byte because the kernel sign-extends bit 55 before printing it.)

The driver source says why8. vdev->queue is one field on the shared video_device, and armcb_v4l2_reqbufs points it at a vb2_queue embedded in a per-open allocation. On close, armcb_v4l2_fop_release clears that pointer only when stream_on_cnt is zero, then frees the allocation either way. Of 2,096 releases in my logs, stream_on_cnt was zero on seven, all of them isp_app closing /dev/video9. Every other close leaves the device pointing into freed memory, and the core reads vdev->queue->lock for any queue ioctl.

The register dump even names the ioctl that walked into it. x20 holds 0xc0405610, which is VIDIOC_EXPBUF, a queue ioctl GStreamer issues while probing whether the node can export dmabufs. The g_selection call logged just before it survived because it isn't a queue ioctl and takes the device mutex instead. So this is a use-after-free on the capture node's queue pointer, caused by a cleanup that the driver's own stream counter skips almost every time. The vendor's /* need fix: hard code for NV12M 1080p fmt */ comment sits inside armcb_v4l2_g_selection, the function that logs the last line before every panic.

Stopping the daemon doesn't help either. With isp-daemon.service stopped and no isp_app running, one capture hung and the next panicked two seconds later, with the same trace. The bug is in the kernel driver, and without the daemon there's no fallback path, just nothing.

docs.title: Why the architecture makes it worse
docs.text:
A buggy driver can happen to anyone. The shape of this stack makes it worse.

The driver is the only meeting point for parties that don't know about each other: the client, the daemon that holds the node permanently, and every other program that opens video devices. The vendor image runs a full desktop, so there are plenty of those: wireplumber, v4l_id, gst-plugin-scan, gst-launch-1.0, v4l2-ctl and isp_app itself, anywhere from 15 to over a thousand closes per boot. Only the daemon's own closes are counted. Everyone else's prints stream_on_cnt:-1, and that's exactly the gap the panic falls through. On the Pi, one process owns the session and the V4L2 core tracks it. Here the driver keeps its own per-stream state for a client it doesn't configure and a daemon it reaches only through events.

Nothing is standard either. No graph, no pad operations, no controls: libcamera can't drive it, my own code can't set exposure, and when something breaks no standard tool can show the state, because it lives in a closed binary and a private struct.

Then supportability. Neither isp_app nor its unit belongs to a package, so nothing updates or removes them, and isp-daemon.service is sloppy:

[Unit]
Description=ISP Daemon
After=network.target load-isp-modules.service

[Service]
Type=simple
Environment=LD_LIBRARY_PATH="/usr/share/cix/lib"
ExecStart=/usr/bin/isp_app -s 0 &
Restart=always
RestartSec=1
StartLimitInterval=10
StartLimitBurst=5

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

systemd doesn't use a shell, so that & reaches the binary as a literal argument, and load-isp-modules.service doesn't exist on the image. Worse, the daemon's stdout goes to journald rather than a tty, so glibc fully buffers it. On one boot journald stamped a line at 14:10 that the daemon itself had timestamped 03:32, ten and a half hours earlier, and delays of several minutes are routine. Lining a crash up with daemon activity is hard when the logs arrive that late.

docs.title: The line that actually matters
docs.text:
It's tempting to read this as "closed daemon bad, open library good". That's the wrong line: libcamera itself runs closed IPAs in a separate process. Neither the process boundary nor closed 3A is the problem.

The line is what the kernel describes. On the Pi 5 it describes the sensor, the links, the formats and the controls through mainline interfaces, so userspace is replaceable and a session lives as long as one process. On the Orange Pi 6 Plus the kernel is a privileged I²C pipe and a buffer manager, the hardware description lives in a closed binary, and the contract between them is a private ioctl whose number collides with another one. The rest follows: no libcamera, no controls, state spread across processes that never talk, and a driver that panics the kernel with or without the daemon.

Nothing here says the CIX ISP silicon is bad. It says the software contract around it was written for exactly one closed client. Until CIX ships a driver that builds a graph, the reliable camera interface on my Orange Pi is its USB port.

docs.title: Video Streaming
docs.text:
Sensor to display, on two boards that disagree about how to do it.

The Raspberry Pi 5 has a clean upstream kernel stack, a walkable media graph, a hardware ISP reachable through libcamera — and no video encoder at all. The Orange Pi 6 Plus has a Linlon V8 that sustains eighteen 1080p30 encode sessions, and a closed vendor daemon that resets the board on four of ten MIPI capture runs. Each board does something the other cannot, and that asymmetry decides how the code gets written.

docs.title: Camera Sensor Fundamentals
docs.text:
Photodiodes, Bayer colour filter arrays, bit depth, packed raw formats, rolling shutter, sensor modes, and HDR. The groundwork for everything the capture path does with a frame.

Platform note: All bit-level layouts here assume little-endian byte order. Raspberry Pi 5 (BCM2712, Cortex-A76) is little-endian. Adjust if you port to a big-endian system.

docs.title: How Camera Sensors Work
docs.text:
Pull a raw frame straight off /dev/video0 on the Pi 5 and you don't get a picture. You get a block of 10-bit packed bytes that decodes to a green-tinted grid of garbage. Everything on this page lives between that block and an actual image: how the sensor turns photons into numbers, why those numbers skew green, and how they get crammed into memory.

A sensor is a grid of millions of photodiodes, and each one does the same dumb job. Collect photons during exposure. Let them knock loose some charge. Read the charge out as a voltage. Hand the voltage to an ADC. Four steps, a few million times a frame.

The catch: a photodiode can't see colour. It counts photons, full stop. Red light and blue light of the same intensity hand back the same number. That's the problem the Bayer filter exists to solve.

docs.title: The Bayer Color Filter Array
docs.text:
Kodak's fix, from Bryce Bayer in 1976, is almost insultingly simple. Glue a tiny coloured filter over each photodiode so it only sees one colour. Arrange those filters in a repeating pattern, and you can reconstruct full colour later from the neighbours. That array of filters is the colour filter array, or CFA.

The usual pattern is a 2x2 tile: one red, one blue, and two green on the diagonal. That tile repeats across the whole sensor.

Why two greens? Your eyes care about green more than red or blue. Most of what you perceive as sharpness and brightness rides on the green channel, so doubling it buys more luminance detail where it matters and leaves the colour reconstruction cleaner.

docs.title: Bayer Pattern Variants
docs.text: Not every sensor starts the tile in the same corner. Same four filters, different starting phase, and the debayering code has to know which is which. Get it wrong and red and blue swap, so faces go blue and skies go orange.

docs.title: Pattern Phase and Crop Alignment
docs.text:
Here's a trap that costs people an afternoon. Crop a raw Bayer frame at an odd pixel coordinate and the pattern shifts under you. An RGGB frame cropped at (0, 0) is still RGGB. Crop the same frame at (1, 0) and it reads as GRBG. The mapping for an RGGB base:

Crop origin (x, y) Effective pattern (even, even) RGGB (odd, even) GRBG (even, odd) GBRG (odd, odd) BGGR

So any ROI or pipeline stage that crops raw data has to snap its crop origin to even coordinates on both axes, or you change the pattern without meaning to. If the sensor driver does a hardware crop, check VIDIOC_SELECTION or the pad format rectangle. The driver might shift the rectangle to keep Bayer alignment, or it might not, in which case the reported origin tells you the phase offset you're stuck with.

The parity rule is general. For any base pattern, the effective CFA shifts one position inside the 2x2 tile for each odd step in x or y. The table uses RGGB because that's the IMX708 case. Start from your sensor's real base (BGGR for the IMX477) and apply the same modular shift.

docs.title: Bit Depth: 10-bit vs 12-bit
docs.text:
People argue 10-bit versus 12-bit like it's a quality tier you buy up into. It mostly isn't. Bit depth is how finely you slice the range, not how wide the range is.

Bit depth sets how many brightness levels each pixel can distinguish:

Bit Depth Brightness Levels Max linearly-representable DR 8-bit 256 256:1 (~8 stops) 10-bit 1,024 1,024:1 (~10 stops) 12-bit 4,096 4,096:1 (~12 stops) 14-bit 16,384 16,384:1 (~14 stops)

Dynamic range is a physics property of the sensor: full-well charge capacity over the read noise floor, the brightest signal it can hold against the faintest it can still tell apart. Bit depth doesn't set that. It sets the precision you quantise it with.

The rule that matters: bit depth has to cover at least as many stops as the sensor's native DR. A 10-stop sensor needs 10 bits to keep every distinguishable tone; go lower and you get banding. Go higher and you're spending bits on noise. When the depth exactly matches the native DR, every stop gets an equal slice of the budget:

Bit depth 2^N / N stops Levels per stop Banding 8-bit 256 / 8 32 visible in smooth sky gradients 10-bit 1024 / 10 102 imperceptible 12-bit 4096 / 12 341 very smooth

These hold for any sensor whose native DR equals what the depth can encode. Capture an 8-stop sensor at 10-bit and the extra bits just sit there carrying nothing, banding gets even less likely. Run a sensor whose DR exceeds the depth and the banding shows up first in the shadows, where the steps are widest.

The two Pi sensors: the IMX708 is about 10 stops native, the IMX477 about 12. So 10-bit already captures everything the IMX708 resolves in standard mode. Its HDR mode reaches further, but it does that by merging two exposures and tone-mapping back down to 10-bit, not by adding bits. Grabbing IMX708 standard output at 12 bits buys you bandwidth cost and zero information.

docs.title: Packed and Unpacked Raw Formats
docs.text: This is where the afternoon actually goes. The bytes off the device aren't one neat value per pixel. Pi sensors hand you the MIPI CSI-2 packed layout, RAW10 or RAW12, straight from /dev/video0 on rp1-cfe, and if you read it like a normal array you get noise.

docs.title: 10-bit Packed (MIPI RAW10): 4 pixels in 5 bytes
docs.text:
Four bytes carry the top eight bits of four pixels. The fifth byte mops up the two low bits of each, most significant pixel first.

// Unpack pixel N (N = 0..3) from a 5-byte RAW10 group
uint16_t msbs = static_cast<uint16_t>(byte[N]) << 2;
uint16_t lsbs = (byte[4] >> (N * 2)) & 0x03u;
uint16_t pixelN = msbs | lsbs;   // 10-bit value, range 0..1023

docs.title: 12-bit Packed (MIPI RAW12): 2 pixels in 3 bytes
docs.text:
Two bytes carry the top eight bits of two pixels. The third byte holds both low nibbles: pixel 1 high, pixel 0 low.

// Unpack pixel 0 from a 3-byte RAW12 group
uint16_t msbs = static_cast<uint16_t>(byte[0]) << 4;
uint16_t lsbs = byte[2] & 0x0Fu;
uint16_t pixel0 = msbs | lsbs;   // 12-bit value, range 0..4095
// pixel1: msbs = byte[1] << 4; lsbs = (byte[2] >> 4) & 0x0F;

The byte holding the low bits (byte 4 for RAW10, byte 2 for RAW12) puts pixel 0 at the bottom: bits [1:0] for RAW10, bits [3:0] for RAW12. Get the order backwards and every value is subtly wrong in a way that looks like noise, not a crash, which is why it eats time.

There are unpacked variants too. Drop the P from the FourCC (SRGGB10 instead of SRGGB10P) and each sample sits right-aligned in a 16-bit little-endian word, upper bits zeroed. Trivial to read, but you pay 60% more bandwidth at 10-bit and 33% at 12-bit. The FourCC encodes both axes at once: SRGGB10P is packed 10-bit RGGB, SBGGR12P is packed 12-bit BGGR.

docs.title: Rolling Shutter vs Global Shutter
docs.text:
Every CMOS sensor on a Pi cheats. It doesn't expose the whole frame at once. It scans row by row from the top, and by the time the bottom row starts collecting light, the top row is already read out and reset. The exposure window rolls down the sensor.

A global shutter exposes every row at the same instant and reads them out after. No rolling artefacts, but it needs storage at every pixel, which eats silicon and costs you sensitivity. Both the IMX708 and the IMX477 are rolling-shutter parts, so you live with the artefacts.

You can estimate readout time per mode from controls the driver exposes (see A5 §2.1):

readout_time = active_height × (active_width + hblank) / pixel_rate

Read V4L2_CID_PIXEL_RATE and V4L2_CID_HBLANK at runtime. Don't hard-code them, they change with the mode.

docs.title: What the Roll Actually Does
docs.text:
Skew is the one you'll notice first. The top rows catch a moving subject earlier than the bottom rows, so anything fast leans. At 2304x1296 the IMX708 reads out in roughly 17.9 ms. A lazy 30 deg/s pan tilts the subject about half a degree, invisible. A hard sports whip-pan at 180 deg/s tilts it past three degrees, and now the whole subject leans on screen.

skew_angle_degrees ≈ angular_velocity_deg_per_s × readout_time_s

Slow the mode down and it gets worse fast. Full-resolution at 14fps reads out near 66 ms, so the same pan leans about 3.5 times harder. Then there's wobble, where sinusoidal handshake offsets each row's horizontal position and straight lines go wavy. And flash sync: a flash shorter than the readout lights only a band of rows, which caps sync speed at roughly one over the readout time. Shorter readout, smaller everything. Higher frame-rate modes are the cure.

docs.title: Sensor Modes and Binning
docs.text:
Pi sensors don't give you a free-form crop knob. They expose a handful of fixed modes, each one a specific readout config that trades field of view, resolution, frame rate, and noise. Picking a mode is picking a point in that trade, whether you realise it or not.

The mechanism behind the sub-resolution modes matters. Binning sums adjacent photosites before the ADC. In 2x2 binning, four sites become one output pixel: resolution halves on each axis, the full field of view stays, and sensitivity climbs about 4x, which buys roughly +6 dB SNR while amortising read noise. Line skipping just throws away alternating rows. Same resolution drop, same frame-rate win, none of the sensitivity gain, plus aliasing on fine detail because the skipped rows contributed nothing. The IMX708 and IMX477 bin rather than skip, so that SNR improvement is real and not a spec-sheet fairy tale.

For video, 2304x1296 is the one to reach for: full field of view, far better low-light than full-res, and it fits the 2-lane CSI-2 budget at 56fps.

docs.title: Selecting a Mode
docs.text:
You don't ask for a mode by name. You request a resolution through VIDIOC_S_FMT and the driver snaps to the nearest mode it has.

Finding out what is on offer is harder than it should be, and on a Pi 5 the obvious route does not work. VIDIOC_ENUM_FRAMESIZES on a capture node returns a single stepwise range rather than the sensor's mode list, VIDIOC_ENUM_FRAMEINTERVALS is not implemented by the driver at all, and VIDIOC_G_PARM and VIDIOC_S_PARM are absent with it: all three return ENOTTY. The discrete modes come from the sensor subdev through VIDIOC_SUBDEV_ENUM_FRAME_SIZE, and the frame-rate table comes from libcamera rather than from V4L2. The Linux Camera Stack has the measurements and the reason.

docs.title: HDR Capture
docs.text:
The IMX708 has a dual-exposure staggered HDR mode, and it's worth being clear about what it does before you switch it on. It captures two exposures per frame and merges them, reaching past the sensor's native ~10 stops.

The long exposure is your normal AE-driven shot and holds the shadows and mid-tones. The short one runs at a quarter to an eighth of that and keeps the highlights from clipping. The ISP merges them per pixel by luma: shadows from the long, highlights from the short, a blended seam in between. Out comes a 10-bit frame with roughly 12-plus stops of apparent range.

Note the output is still 10-bit. The extra range lives in the tone curve, not in extra bits, and 10-bit covers the merged 12-stop range at about 341 levels per stop, smooth enough that you won't see steps.

The constraints are where it bites. HDR only works in the 2304x1296 binned mode. Full-res and the 1536x864 120fps mode can't do it, their readout timing has no room for the second exposure. And the second exposure isn't free: that binned mode drops from 56fps to roughly 28 in HDR, because each output frame now needs two sequential captures. Verify the exact rate on your kernel and firmware, since the IPA tuning file can move it. You also pick up motion artefacts at the merge seam when the scene shifts between exposures, and flash sync is gone, because two exposures make the sync geometry inconsistent. You enable the whole thing through libcamera's controls::HdrMode; raw V4L2 won't expose it.

The merged frame feeds the ISP like any other, so nothing about HDR changes what the ISP can do with it downstream. How many outputs that is, and what each one can be configured to, is a question about the ISP back end rather than the sensor, and is not covered here.

The IMX477 has none of this on-sensor. If you want HDR there, you merge sequential frames yourself in the application, and you eat the motion artefacts that come from the scene moving frame to frame.
